note: A crescent dumpling folded around a minced filling. You picture the whole family around the table on New Year's Eve, pinching edges, someone hiding a coin in one for luck.

gloss: (slang) service provider for Shadowsocks or similar software for circumventing Internet censorship
note: Slang for a paid service that sells a way around the Great Firewall. When a friend says they switched 机场, you know they mean their route to Google, not an airport.

The countryside, as the half of China outside city life and city registration. Saying someone grew up in 农村 quietly places them: you hear dirt roads, farm chores and fewer chances, not pretty scenery.
A classmate, and also the polite way to hail any student you don't know. The tie lasts, so decades later being someone's 同学 is still a reason to do them a favour.
Relatives, as a whole web you owe visits to. You picture New Year rounds of aunts and cousins asking how much you earn and when you're getting married.

gloss: form of address used by children for a male one generation older
note: A friendly title a child uses for any man of their parents' generation. You call a friend's dad or the security guard 叔叔, and it signals respect with no family tie at all.

gloss: term of address for a woman of one's mother's generation
note: A warm title for any woman of your mother's generation. Shop assistants, neighbours and a friend's mum all become 阿姨, which keeps things polite and a little familial.
A nanny or childminder, addressed as auntie. Calling her 阿姨 keeps it warm and respectful, though the arrangement is paid work.
A son's wife, seen as having married into his family. You picture a young woman learning the ways of her mother-in-law's house, the classic source of family friction.
A husband's homely word for his wife in the north. It sounds affectionate and down to earth, the way you'd say "the missus" with a smile.
To die, said gently. You hear 他走了 softly in a hospital corridor, a way of saying it without saying the hard word.
Revolutionary, communist. Red songs, red tourism and red classics carry the Party's glow of patriotism and nostalgia, not just a colour.
A person, said with contempt. Calling someone a 东西, as in 你不是东西, turns them into a thing, and it stings.
A small gift or gesture that shows goodwill. You hand over an envelope saying it's just 一点小意思, and everyone understands it's a courtesy, or a gentle nudge.
Personal connections that get things done. You don't just know people, you owe and are owed, and a job found 靠关系 means somebody cashed in a favour.
Good enough, close enough. It can be an easy-going shrug, or a dig at the famous Mr About-Right, 差不多先生, who never quite bothers to get things right.
Whatever you like. When a host says 随便 it's generous, but when your partner says 随便 about where to eat, you know no answer will be right.

gloss: to go to a lot of trouble
note: To go to a lot of trouble for something. You say 辛苦了 to the courier or a colleague at the end of a long day, a small bow to the effort they put in.

gloss: to bother sb; to put sb to trouble
note: To put someone to trouble, used as a polite ask. Saying 麻烦你 before a request admits you're about to put them out, and softens it.
Polite in a holding-back way. When a friend says 别客气 they mean drop the ceremony, because being too 客气 with someone close feels cold.
Lively in the good, crowded, noisy way. You picture a packed restaurant, firecrackers and everyone talking at once, and that's exactly what makes it feel happy.
Wronged, and having to swallow it. You picture a child with trembling lips who did nothing wrong but got blamed anyway.
To ache for someone. Your chest tightens seeing your mum work too hard; it's love felt as a small pain.
To hate losing or spending something. You wince at a cracked new phone or a wasted meal, and that wince is 心疼.
Can't bear to let go. You linger at the station hugging your grandma, or keep a worn jacket you'll never wear again.
Sorry for the bother, said lightly. You say it squeezing past someone or asking a favour, half apology and half embarrassment.

gloss: section of society operating independently of mainstream society, out of reach of the law; the milieu in which wuxia tales play out (cf. 武俠|武侠[wu3 xia2])
note: The world outside respectable society, where reputation and loyalty rule. You picture wandering swordsmen, and later anyone living by their wits beyond official rules.
Social face: the standing other people grant you. You insist on paying the bill to give a friend 面子, and contradicting your boss in public makes him lose it.
A favour owed. Accepting help means you now carry a 人情, and you'll be expected to repay it, maybe years later.

gloss: a connection (sb with whom one has dealings on the basis of "scratch my back and I'll scratch yours")
note: Someone who got their place through connections. Coworkers say it under their breath about the new hire nobody remembers interviewing.

gloss: (fig.) to pull strings; to use connections
note: To get something through connections instead of the official way. You picture a quiet word, a dinner, a gift, and suddenly the hospital bed is free.

gloss: devoted to one's parents (and grandparents etc)
note: Devoted and obedient to your parents, as a moral duty. It's not just loving them; you're expected to support them, defer to them and give them grandchildren.

gloss: fate or chance that brings people together
note: The pull of fate that brings two people together. Running into an old friend in a foreign city, you smile and say it's 缘分.
Vital energy, the life force of traditional medicine and martial arts. You picture breath, warmth and strength flowing through the body, and illness as that flow getting stuck.

gloss: to suffer from excessive internal heat (TCM)
note: In traditional medicine, too much internal heat in the body. After spicy hotpot you get a sore throat and mouth ulcers, and your mum hands you herbal tea because you've 上火.
To build up the body with nourishing food or tonics. Grandma ladles you chicken soup after an illness because you need to 补.
Your household registration, tied to where your family is officially from. It decides which school your child can attend and whether a city ever fully counts you as its own.

gloss: work unit (place of employment, esp. in the PRC prior to economic reform)
note: Your work unit: once the employer that also handed out housing, medical care and permission to marry. People still say 我们单位 with that sense of an institution owning part of your life.
A job you can't lose, usually in the state sector. Parents dream of it for their children: never rich, never fired.

gloss: (fig.) to take the plunge (e.g. leave a secure job, or enter prostitution etc)
note: To quit a secure state job and go into business. It recalls the 1990s rush when officials and teachers jumped into private trade.

gloss: (of a worker) be to laid off
note: Laid off, especially from a state factory during the 1990s reforms. It brings back millions of workers suddenly without the jobs they'd been promised for life.

gloss: (neologism, attested by 2017) (of a society) to become more and more of a rat race; to become increasingly competitive (due to limited resources)
note: Pointless, exhausting competition where everyone works harder and nobody gets ahead. You feel it when classmates start studying at 5 a.m. only because others do.

gloss: (neologism, attested by 2021) to opt out of the rat race
note: To lie flat: quietly opt out of the rat race. It's a shrug against 内卷, choosing a modest life over wearing yourself out for a promotion.

gloss: (fig.) to loaf on the job; to be slack; to take it easy
note: To slack off at work. You picture someone scrolling their phone under the desk, feeling they've stolen a little time back.

gloss: (neologism, attested by 2017) (coll.) chill about everything (typically used to describe young people who don't buy into aspirational society)
note: Chill about everything, like a calm Buddhist monk. You don't push and don't compete, and whatever happens is fine.
To endure hardship, seen as a virtue. Parents praise a child who 能吃苦, and suffering is treated as proof of character.
Ordinary people, as opposed to officials. You mean the folks who just get on with their lives while decisions are made above them.
Intellectuals, as a social class with a duty to the nation. The word carries a long history, from honoured scholars to targets of political campaigns.
A Party or state cadre: someone with a position in the system. You picture the official in a work unit or village whose signature gets things done.
The masses, in political language. It's the people as a whole that the Party says it serves, and officials are told to "go among the masses".
Comrade: the old revolutionary address between equals. Today it sounds official or nostalgic, and it is also a word gay people use for themselves.
Revolution, above all the Communist one. The word carries a heroic, almost sacred glow from decades of Party history and textbooks.

gloss: reform and opening up (Chinese policy introduced in 1978)
note: Reform and opening up, the move to markets that began in 1978. People use it to mark the line between the poor, closed China of their parents and the boom since.

gloss: educated youth (esp. those sent to work in rural areas during the Cultural Revolution) (abbr. for 知識青年|知识青年[zhi1 shi5 qing1 nian2])
note: City youth sent to work in the countryside during the Cultural Revolution. You think of a whole generation who lost their schooling and still tell stories of those villages.

gloss: forced agricultural experience for city intellectuals
note: The campaign sending city teenagers to labour in the countryside in the 1960s and 70s. You picture trains of young people heading to remote farms, many staying for a decade.

gloss: migrant worker (who moved from a rural area of China to a city to find work)
note: Rural migrant workers in the cities. You picture men on building sites and women in factories, far from children left back home, without city registration.

gloss: to work a temporary or casual job
note: To work for someone else, especially a casual or migrant job. Every year young people from the countryside 出去打工, leaving villages to the old and the very young.
A wage slave, said with ironic self-pity. Office workers call themselves 打工人 to joke about grinding away for a boss.

gloss: (increased) passenger transportation around Chinese New Year
note: The Spring Festival travel rush. You picture packed trains, people standing for twenty hours and tickets gone in seconds, all to get home for New Year.

gloss: money wrapped in red as a gift
note: A red envelope of money given at New Year, weddings and other happy occasions. Children collect them from relatives, and adults feel the pressure of giving the right amount.
A cash gift slipped to a doctor or official for better treatment. Everyone knows what it means when a 红包 changes hands before surgery.

gloss: to celebrate the Chinese New Year
note: To celebrate Chinese New Year. It means going home, the family dinner, red envelopes and noise; missing it feels like missing the whole year.

gloss: Pure Brightness Festival or Tomb Sweeping Day (in early April)
note: Tomb Sweeping Day in early April. Families visit graves, tidy them and burn paper offerings for the dead.
Ancestors, as a family line owed respect. Shaming yourself shames the 祖宗, whose graves and tablets are tended for generations.
The motherland, said with patriotic warmth. It's the word of school songs and National Day, full of pride and duty.
Your family's place of origin, where your roots are. Even if you grew up in Shanghai, your 老家 might be a village you visit once a year.
Homesickness and longing for the place you came from. It's the ache of an emigrant looking at the moon and thinking of a village far away.

gloss: in old age, an expatriate returns home
note: To return home in old age. You picture an elderly emigrant who wants to be buried in the village of their ancestors.
Filial piety: the Confucian duty to honour and care for your parents. It's the moral bedrock of family life, not just affection.
Propriety: the Confucian order of correct behaviour. It's knowing who pours tea for whom, who sits where, and how to show respect without being told.
Humaneness, the central Confucian virtue. It's kindness rooted in your relationships, the mark of a truly good person.
Righteousness: doing what's right even when it costs you. It's the loyalty of sworn brothers in old novels who'd die for each other.
The Dao, the Way of things in Daoism. It's the natural flow of the world that can't be named, only followed.
A person of noble character, the Confucian gentleman. You picture someone principled and composed, the opposite of a petty 小人.
A petty, scheming person. You picture a coworker who smiles to your face and undermines you behind your back.
All under heaven: the whole world as one realm under a ruler. It carries the ancient sense of China as the civilised centre of everything.
State power, the realm held by a ruler or a party. When people say someone 打江山, they mean they fought to win the country.
A nation or ethnic group. In China it covers both the 56 official ethnic groups and the idea of one Chinese nation.
To love one's country. It's taught as a core duty from school onward, and can feel both heartfelt and expected.

gloss: respectful form of address for older men
note: A respectful address for a skilled worker or an older man. You call the taxi driver or the plumber 师傅, and they feel properly respected.
Boss or owner, and also a flattering way to address a customer. Street vendors call you 老板 to make you feel important.
To be particular about doing things properly. A family that 讲究 about food cares about season, region and how it's served; it reads as refinement, not fussiness.
To make do with less than you'd like. You squeeze into a small flat and tell yourself it will do for now.
To just about get by. Asked how life is, you say 凑合 with a shrug: not great, not terrible.

gloss: to repeat sth over and over again
note: To keep fussing and changing things for no good reason. Moving house three times in a year is 瞎折腾, and everyone is worn out.
To work overtime, often unpaid and expected. In tech jobs it's part of 996 culture: 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., six days a week.
Your boss or superior, especially in an office or state body. You say 领导 even for a middle manager, and everyone knows to laugh at their jokes at dinner.
A sex worker, in slang. Because of this, calling a waitress 小姐 can now sound insulting, so people say 服务员 or 美女 instead.
A beautiful woman, and also a casual way to hail any young woman. A shop assistant calling you 美女 is just being friendly, not flirting.
Handsome, as a casual way to address any young man. A street vendor shouts 帅哥 to get your attention, whatever you look like.
A teacher, in an older and more reverent sense. Calling a great scholar 先生, as people do for Lu Xun, gives them deep respect.

gloss: fellow townsman; fellow villager; sb from the same hometown
note: Someone from your home town or province. Meeting a 老乡 far from home, you switch to dialect and instantly feel you're on the same side.
A buddy, a mate. Calling someone 哥们 claims easy male loyalty: you'd help each other move house, no questions asked.
A woman's closest female friend. She's the one who hears everything first and judges your boyfriends ruthlessly.
A boyfriend or girlfriend, usually with marriage in view. Relatives ask 有对象了吗 at New Year, and it isn't small talk.

gloss: arranged interview to evaluate a proposed marriage partner (Taiwan pr. [xiang4 qin1])
note: A meeting arranged to size up a possible spouse. You picture a stiff coffee with a stranger your aunt found, each side checking job, flat and family.

gloss: (coll.) "leftover woman" – a woman who remains single beyond the typical marrying age
note: A "leftover woman": single and over about 27. The label stings, and many women have taken it back with defiant humour.
Money or gifts the groom's family pays the bride's family. In some regions the sum can be enormous, and haggling over it can sink an engagement.
Your husband's mother. You picture the classic tension of a new wife living under her mother-in-law's eye.
Your wife's mother, the person a groom must win over. Jokes say a man needs a flat and a car before the 丈母娘 will even meet him.

gloss: (of a prospective marriage partner) an appropriate match
note: A match between families of equal standing. Parents still weigh jobs, wealth and background, and a mismatch can end a romance.

gloss: to carry on one's ancestral line
note: To carry on the family line, traditionally through a son. You feel the quiet pressure from grandparents who want a grandson to keep the surname going.

gloss: (of parents) to bring up children for the purpose of being looked after in old age
note: Raising children so they'll look after you in old age. It's the old social contract: no pension, but your son will take you in.

gloss: to bring honor to one's ancestors
note: To bring glory to your ancestors. Passing the exam or getting rich is a win for the whole family line, not just you.

gloss: lit. to hope one's son becomes a dragon (idiom); fig. to long for one' s child to succeed in life
note: Hoping your child will become a dragon. You picture parents spending everything on tutoring so their child can rise above them.

gloss: college entrance exam (especially as abbr. for 普通高等學校招生全國統一考試|普通高等学校招生全国统一考试[Pu3 tong1 Gao1 deng3 Xue2 xiao4 Zhao1 sheng1 Quan2 guo2 Tong3 yi1 Kao3 shi4])
note: The national university entrance exam. It's two days in June that can decide a teenager's whole future, and the country goes quiet around exam halls.

gloss: top scorer in college entrance examination 高考[gao1 kao3]
note: The top scorer in a province's 高考. The 状元 is celebrated in the news, a name echoing the old imperial exam champions.

gloss: to sit an entrance exam for a graduate program
note: To sit the national exam for postgraduate study. You picture a year of library mornings, flashcards and anxiety among millions of rivals.

gloss: sb who has come back to China after gaining overseas experience (a pun on 海龜|海龟[hai3 gui1])
note: Someone who's come back to China after studying or working abroad. The term once meant prized talent; now a foreign degree is less of a golden ticket.
A star student who seems to effortlessly top every exam. Everyone copies the 学霸's notes and secretly resents them a little.

gloss: (neologism, c. 2020) to arrange an intensive schedule of activities for one's child to maximize achievement
note: To push a child through an intense schedule of classes and activities. You picture a nine-year-old with Olympiad maths, piano and English on a Saturday.
A cram school for extra tutoring outside school. Evenings and weekends disappear into them, all to gain a few more exam points.
A key school or project, ranked as top tier. A 重点 high school feeds the best universities, and parents move house to get their child in.

gloss: (of an education system) to be exam-oriented
note: Exam-oriented, as in an education built to pass tests. People say 应试教育 to complain about rote learning that kills curiosity.
A person's inner quality and manners. Saying someone has no 素质 for littering or queue-jumping is a sharp public judgement.
The system: the state apparatus and its jobs. Working 体制内, inside the system, means stability and rules; outside it means risk and freedom.

gloss: authorized staffing allocation in government or public institutions (excluding temporary or contract staff)
note: An official, permanent post in a government or public body. Getting 编制 is the dream of security, and young people take exam after exam for one.
Fate, the life you were dealt. People sigh 这就是命 when hardship seems unavoidable, half acceptance, half complaint.
Blessing and good fortune. You see the character stuck upside down on doors at New Year, because 倒 sounds like "arrived".
Good fortune as something you're blessed with. Grandparents surrounded by grandchildren are said to have real 福气.
Karmic retribution. When a cheat finally gets caught, people say 报应 with a sense of cosmic justice.
The Buddhist cycle of death and rebirth. You picture souls passing through lives over and over until they escape.

gloss: to devote oneself to spiritual development (esp. Buddhism or Daoism)
note: Spiritual practice, especially Buddhist or Daoist. It also means living with discipline and patience, as if daily life were a path.
Merit earned through good deeds, in Buddhist belief. Donating to a temple or freeing captive fish is said to add 功德.
Strength of character with a certain dignity. You picture a scholar who stays upright and refuses to flatter power.
Moral integrity under pressure. It's the official who would rather die than serve an invader.
Backbone: refusing to bow or beg. A poor man who won't accept charity on humiliating terms has 骨气.
Upright moral spirit. Someone full of 正气 stands up against wrongdoing, and you can feel it in the room.
Loyalty among friends that may require sacrifice. It's the code of sworn brothers who stand by each other even against the law.
To stick by your friends. A friend who 讲义气 will lend you money without asking why.
The feelings and face of a relationship. Refusing a request from an old classmate is hard because you want to save 情面.
To exchange polite pleasantries. Everyone knows the compliments at dinner are 客套, not meant to be taken literally.
Business entertaining: banquets and drinking with clients or officials. You picture a tired husband coming home late smelling of baijiu.

gloss: to toast; to propose a toast
note: To toast someone, especially a senior, to show respect. You stand, lower your glass below theirs and drink, round after round.
Cheers! Literally "dry the cup", and you're expected to finish it, not sip.
To invite someone and pay. Friends tussle at the till over who gets to 请客, because paying shows generosity and face.

gloss: to pay the bill; to pick up the tab
note: To pay the bill, and by extension to take responsibility. When people ask who will 买单 for a failed policy, they mean who pays the price.
Your network of connections. In business you're judged by your 人脉 as much as your skills.
Your social circle, often closed and hard to enter. Breaking into a new 圈子 means banquets, introductions and favours.
To muddle through life, getting by. Asking 你混得怎么样 is how old friends ask how life's treating you, with a wry grin.
To lose out, get the short end of the stick. Parents tell kids 吃亏是福, losing out now is a blessing, to teach patience.
To take unfair advantage. You picture someone grabbing extra free samples or never paying their share.
To restrain yourself and endure. The character shows a knife over a heart, and swallowing your anger is seen as wisdom.
Frustrated and holding it in. You feel it when you can't talk back to your boss, the anger stuck in your chest.
Feeling helpless and humiliated. You're bullied but can't fight back, and you hate yourself a little for it.
Keeping a low profile. A rich man who 低调 drives a plain car, and modesty is admired.
To make modest remarks, playing down your success. When praised you say 哪里哪里, and accepting praise too readily seems arrogant.

gloss: (of a person or style etc) reserved
note: Reserved, saying things indirectly. Feelings are hinted, not declared, and a 含蓄 person might never say "I love you".
Tactful, softening things. You say 不太方便 instead of no, and everyone understands.
Naive, easily taken advantage of. Calling a man 老实 can be praise for honesty or a sigh that he'll be exploited.
Smooth and evasive. You picture someone who never offends anyone and never commits to anything.
Worldly-wise, in a calculating way. A 世故 person knows exactly whom to please, and it's not quite a compliment.
Honest and down to earth. You trust a 实在 person: what they say is what they mean, and they'll give you a fair price.
Reliable, sensible. A 靠谱 friend shows up on time and does what they promised.
Absurd, way off. You hear about a crazy price or a wild rumour and say 太离谱了.
A weirdo, an oddball. You call a colleague who brings a fish to the office microwave a 奇葩.
Unsophisticated, uncool. Calling someone's clothes 土 means they look rural and old-fashioned.
Trendy, with a foreign flair. Calling an outfit 洋气 is a compliment, linking stylish with Western.
Down to earth, in touch with ordinary people. A politician eating at a street stall to look 接地气 is the image.

gloss: to act like a spoiled child; to act coquettishly
note: To act cute and whiny to get your way. You picture a girl pouting and tugging her boyfriend's sleeve.
Affected, making a fuss over nothing. Complaining about a tiny inconvenience for an hour is 矫情.
High-maintenance, causing drama on purpose. A girlfriend who picks fights to test her partner is 作.

gloss: (coll.) presenting as unfriendly and blunt, but warm and tender inside (loanword from Japanese "tsundere")
note: Acting cold while secretly caring. It's the anime-style character who blushes while saying they don't like you.
Emotionally drained. After dealing with family drama, you just say 心累.
Speechless, exasperated. When a friend does something ridiculous, you just type 无语.

gloss: to struggle (mentally) with (sth); to overthink; to feel conflicted
note: Torn, overthinking a decision. You go back and forth between two flats for weeks, completely 纠结.
To die of embarrassment in public. You trip on stage at graduation and know you've had a 社死 moment.

gloss: (slang) to break through sb's emotional defenses; to get to sb emotionally
note: To have your emotional guard broken. A touching video makes you suddenly tear up, and you say 我破防了.

gloss: (slang) to compete to an unhealthy degree; hypercompetitive
note: To compete to an unhealthy degree. If colleagues stay until midnight, you're all being 卷.

gloss: (neologism, attested by 2014) (slang) to stop striving (esp. when one knows one cannot succeed); to let it all go to hell; (sports) to tank
note: To stop trying because it's hopeless anyway. A student who gives up on exams and plays games is 摆烂.
Awesome, impressive. You say 太牛了 when a friend pulls off something amazing.
Northeast China, the old industrial heartland. It brings to mind snow, plain-spoken humour and the decline of state factories.
A court eunuch in imperial China. You picture powerful palace insiders, often hated, who served the emperor up close.
The imperial civil service exams, used for over a thousand years. Passing them could lift a family from poverty into the ruling class.

gloss: a person who has passed the county level imperial exam (historical)
note: Someone who passed the county-level imperial exam. It meant scholarly status, and today calls up a bookish, impractical young man.

gloss: yamen, government office in dynastic China
note: The government office of imperial China, where the magistrate held court. People still say it sarcastically about bureaucratic offices.
An upright, incorruptible official. People longed for a 青天 like Judge Bao who would right injustices against the powerful.
A knight-errant who defends the weak. You picture a wandering swordsman who rights wrongs outside the law.

gloss: martial arts chivalry (Chinese literary, theatrical and cinema genre)
note: The martial arts genre of fiction and film. You picture flying swordsmen, secret techniques and codes of honour.
A brave, upstanding man. Calling someone a 好汉 echoes the outlaw heroes of the Water Margin.
To plunder. It carries a sense of organised, violent seizure, the way an army strips a land.
Colonial rule. It brings up foreign powers carving up China, a wound in the national memory.
Humiliating, a deep wound to pride. You feel the national shame of past defeats taught in history class.

gloss: national humiliation, refers to Japanese incursions into China in the 1930s and 40s, and more especially to Mukden railway incident of 18th September 1931 九一八事變|九一八事变 and subsequent Japanese annexation of Manchuria
note: National humiliation, especially at the hands of Japan and the West. It's a lesson repeated in schools so the past is never forgotten.

gloss: war of resistance, especially the war against Japan (1937-1945)
note: The War of Resistance against Japan, 1937 to 1945. It's the war of family stories, films and memorial days.

gloss: refers to the Communists' victory over the Nationalists in 1949
note: Liberation: the Communist victory in 1949. People date things 解放前 or 解放后, before or after it.
The rise of a power. China's 崛起 is spoken of with pride, a nation standing up after a century of weakness.
To censor, in slang. A post that gets 被和谐了 has been quietly deleted.
Stability, as a political priority. Leaders say 稳定压倒一切: stability above all else.
Maintaining social stability. It means the state apparatus that heads off protests before they start.
Positivity, especially the upbeat content officials and media promote. Calling a story 正能量 can be sincere praise or a wink at propaganda.

gloss: (of a movie) created with the purpose of promoting Party values and point of view
note: A film or show made to promote the Party line. You expect patriotic heroes, a stirring score and a predictable ending.
Propaganda or publicity, without the sinister edge it has elsewhere. A 宣传部 is a normal publicity department, and posters on every street are 宣传.
The collective, valued above the individual. From school onward you're taught to put the group first, and 集体荣誉 is a real feeling.

gloss: to close a country to exclude foreign contact
note: To close the country to foreign contact. It brings up the Ming and Qing sea bans, a shorthand for how China fell behind the West.

gloss: a person with knowledge and experience (idiom)
note: People of insight and conscience. It implies a duty: if you see clearly, you are bound to speak up.
So-so, passable. Asked how your exam went, you say 马马虎虎 with a shrug, which might mean anything from fine to bad.

gloss: lit. draw legs on a snake (idiom); fig. to ruin the effect by adding sth superfluous
note: To ruin something by adding unnecessary details. It comes from a story about a man who lost a bet by drawing feet on his snake.
To wait passively for good luck. From the farmer who saw a rabbit break its neck on a stump and then waited by it forever.
To fix things after the damage is done, but better late than never. From the shepherd who mended his pen after losing a sheep, to save the rest.
To contradict yourself. From the merchant who claimed his spear could pierce anything and his shield could stop anything.

gloss: fig. offering a treat to an unappreciative audience
note: To waste your words on someone who can't appreciate them. You picture a musician serenading a cow that just keeps chewing.

gloss: (fig.) a person of limited outlook and experience
note: Someone with a narrow view of the world. From a frog at the bottom of a well who thinks the sky is the size of the opening.
A blessing in disguise. From the old man who lost his horse, which came back leading another, a story about fortune's twists.

gloss: (fig.) to maintain one's resolve for revenge
note: To endure hardship while nursing your resolve for revenge. From a defeated king who slept on brushwood and licked bitter gall to remember his shame.

gloss: fig. to console oneself with illusions
note: To console yourself with an illusion. From soldiers who stopped feeling thirsty when told of a plum grove ahead.

gloss: lit. the fox exploits the tiger's might (idiom); fig. to use powerful connections to intimidate people

gloss: lit. a notch on the side of a boat to locate a sword dropped overboard (idiom); fig. an action made pointless by changed circumstances

gloss: to spoil things through excessive enthusiasm (idiom)

gloss: a crane in a flock of chicken (idiom); way above the common

gloss: to give up halfway (idiom); leave sth unfinished
note: To give up halfway. Parents say it to children who quit piano after a month, a mild reproach.

gloss: fig. to be practical and realistic
note: To seek truth from facts. It's also a famous Party slogan, so you hear it in official speeches about being practical.

gloss: as it should be by rights (idiom); proper and to be expected as a matter of course
note: Taken for granted as right. It's often used to criticise people who see others' help as their due.

gloss: (idiom) baffling; bizarre; without rhyme or reason; inexplicable
note: Baffling, makes no sense. You say it when a colleague snaps at you for no reason.

gloss: May you have a prosperous New Year! (New Year's greeting)
note: The New Year greeting wishing wealth. Children reply 红包拿来, give me a red envelope, as a joke.

gloss: (idiom) when in Rome, do as the Romans do
note: When in a new place, follow local customs. You say it when trying strange food on a trip.

gloss: to fall in love at first sight (idiom)

gloss: (idiom) of long standing; with a long history; stretching back to ancient times
note: Long-standing, with deep roots. It's a set phrase about Chinese civilisation's continuous history.

gloss: to endure humiliation as part of an important mission (idiom); to suffer in silence
note: To bear humiliation for an important mission. You picture someone swallowing insults to protect a greater cause.

gloss: to abandon self for others (idiom, from Analects); to sacrifice one's own interest for other people

gloss: a hundred schools of thought contend (idiom); refers to the classical philosophic schools of the Warring States period 475-221 BC

gloss: a hundred flowers bloom (idiom); let the arts have free expression

gloss: to keep up with the times
note: To keep up with the times. It's an official slogan, so it can sound earnest or bureaucratic.

gloss: to live in peace and work happily (idiom)
note: To live in peace and work happily. It's the old ideal of a well-governed land.

gloss: to win top marks in the imperial examinations
note: To pass the imperial exam with honours. Today it's a wish for success in the 高考.

gloss: fig. to study diligently in the face of hardship
note: To study despite hardship. From a poor boy who drilled a hole in the wall to read by his neighbour's light.

gloss: to start practicing at the first crow of the cock (idiom)

gloss: fig. surrounded by enemies, isolated and without help
note: Surrounded by enemies with no help. From a besieged general who heard his homeland's songs from the enemy camp.

gloss: fig. to regroup and come back even stronger
note: To come back stronger after defeat. You picture a defeated army gathering its dust to return.

gloss: lit. fight with one's back to the river (idiom); fig. to fight to win or die

gloss: lit. to return the jade annulus to Zhao (idiom); fig. to return something intact to its rightful owner
note: To return something intact to its owner. From the minister who safely brought a precious jade back to the state of Zhao.

gloss: fig. to offer sb a humble apology
note: To offer a humble apology. From a general who carried thorns on his back to beg forgiveness from a minister.

gloss: fig. to make earnest and repeated requests of sb
note: To repeatedly and sincerely invite someone. From Liu Bei visiting Zhuge Liang's hut three times to win him over.

A sea of people. You picture the West Lake on a public holiday, packed shoulder to shoulder.

gloss: to amaze the world with a single brilliant feat (idiom); an overnight celebrity

gloss: not feel ashamed to ask and learn from one's subordinates
note: Not ashamed to learn from those below you. It's praise from Confucius for humble learning.

Your husband's mother. You picture the classic tension of a new wife living under her mother-in-law's eye.

note: To part, often for a long time. It feels heavier than saying goodbye, and you use it for people you may not see for years.
Model, award-worthy. 先进工作者 is an official workplace honor, and you picture a certificate and a red banner.
The top leadership in Beijing. When you hear 中央 on its own you think of the Party Central Committee, and a document from it feels final.

gloss: people's congress, a legislative body within the PRC's system of government at any of various levels – national, provincial, municipal, county or township (abbr. for 人民代表大會|人民代表大会[ren2 min2 dai4 biao3 da4 hui4])
note: The people's congress, China's legislature. You picture the Great Hall of the People each March, and you don't expect a surprise vote.
Your way of thinking, and your politics. When someone does your 思想工作 they're talking you round, at home as much as at work.
A formality, something done for show. With 走形式 you go through the motions, and everyone in the room knows it.
To argue it out and demand fairness. 找他理论 means you march over to have it out with someone who wronged you.
Sensible, done properly. When you say 这不科学 you're half joking, meaning this just makes no sense.
Lively, sharp, well turned out. You say 真精神 to a young man with a new haircut, and it's about the whole look of being awake and alive.

gloss: in the end; as a result
note: In the end, and often not how you hoped. In a story 结果 warns you of the letdown, as in 我等了一天，结果他没来.
To serve. You see 为人民服务 on signs at government offices, and depending on the day at the counter you read it straight or with a sigh.
Socialism, and for you a word from school and slogans. You memorized the twelve words of 社会主义核心价值观 and still see them on street banners.
A political campaign. If you lived through the Mao years, 运动 on its own means the next round of denunciations, and hearing one is coming makes you uneasy.
